bib.title: Statistical Inference and Methodology in the Postwar Era (Chapter 14, Computer Age Statistical Inference)

question: How do the fifteen postwar methodology topics of Part II line up against the Bayesian, frequentist and Fisherian philosophies, and how much did electronic computation matter to each?
contributions: A scorecard of 15 topics by inferential affinity and computational importance (Figure 14.1)
Updated version of Figure 8 in Efron (1998)

results.quote: the speed of computation increased by a factor of a thousand, and then another thousand

limits: Authors say the placement is not very precise.
Objective Bayes is hard to place; Lehmann argues for a more frequentist position and the figure does not act on it.
Figure positions and colours are judgments, not measurements; the figure's coordinates are not in the text layer.
Chapter is a summary and defers all detail to Chapters 6-13.
practices: Read each method by its inferential affinity (Bayes, frequentist, Fisher) and its computational demand, not by era alone (Fig 14.1, p265).

Treat bootstrap, MCMC, regression trees and (later) machine learning as computer-intensive; treat BIC, AIC, Cp, Kaplan-Meier, James-Stein as designed to avoid or not need heavy computation (pp265-267).

figures.caption: Bayesian, frequentist, and Fisherian influences, as described in the text, on 15 major topics, 1950s through 1990s. Colors indicate the importance of electronic computation in their development: red, crucial; violet, very important; green, important; light blue, less important; blue, negligible.
figures.why: Triangle places 15 methods by philosophy and computation at once; the one-glance map of Part II

problems: Text layer is only 7134 chars; Figure 14.1 colours and coordinates exist only in the image, so per-topic colours not stated in prose are unconfirmed.
